summary.text: Writing $m=(p-1)/2$, Wilson’s theorem gives $(m!)^2=-1$ for $p\equiv1\pmod4$; after Euler’s criterion rewrites the entries modulo $p$ as $(i^2-m!j)^m$, interpolation at the distinct nodes $1^2,\ldots,m^2$ and binomial moment identities rule out a nonzero kernel. For $p\equiv3\pmod4$, where $m$ is odd and $m!\equiv\varepsilon=\pm1$, the same interpolation method makes the auxiliary matrix $(\chi(i^2+\varepsilon j))$ invertible, while quadratic-character sum identities make its transpose-product with the original matrix skew-symmetric, forcing the original determinant to vanish.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p=p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, where \(n\geq 2\), and put
\[
 m=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad C=m!.
\]
Since \(n\geq2\), we have \(p\geq3\), so \(p\) is odd and \(2m=p-1\). Let
\[
 A=(A_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq m},\qquad
 A_{ij}=\left(\frac{i^2-Cj}{p}\right).
\]
Thus the sequence term in question is \(a(n)=\det A\). We prove that
\[
 \det A=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
Throughout, write \(\mathbb F_p\) for the field with \(p\) elements and \(\chi\) for its quadratic character, extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). We use the same letters for ordinary integers and their residue classes in \(\mathbb F_p\).

## 1. Preliminary facts

### The value of \((m!)^2\)

Wilson's theorem gives
\[
 (p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p.
\]
Pairing the factors \(m+1,\ldots,p-1\) with \(-m,\ldots,-1\), we obtain
\[
 (p-1)!=m!\prod_{r=1}^{m}(p-r)
 \equiv m!\prod_{r=1}^{m}(-r)
 =(-1)^m(m!)^2\pmod p.
\]
Consequently
\[
 C^2=(m!)^2=(-1)^{m+1}\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{1}
\]
In particular,
\[
 \begin{cases}
 C^2=-1,&p\equiv1\pmod4,\\
 C^2=1,&p\equiv3\pmod4.
 \end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(p=4r+1\), then \(m=2r\), whereas if \(p=4r+3\), then \(m=2r+1\). Notice also that \(C\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), since every factor of \(m!\) is strictly between \(0\) and \(p\).

### Distinct interpolation nodes

The elements \(1,2,\ldots,m\) are distinct and nonzero in \(\mathbb F_p\). Their squares are also distinct. For if \(i^2=j^2\), then \(i=j\) or \(i=-j\). The latter would imply \(i+j=p\) as ordinary positive integers, but
\[
 2\leq i+j\leq2m=p-1,
\]
which is impossible. Thus
\[
 1^2,2^2,\ldots,m^2
\]
are \(m\) distinct elements of \(\mathbb F_p\). Fermat's theorem also gives
\[
 (i^2)^m=i^{2m}=i^{p-1}=1\qquad(1\leq i\leq m). \tag{3}
\]
Hence these \(m\) nodes are roots of \(X^m-1\).

We shall also use the usual Vandermonde consequence: if \(u_1,\ldots,u_m\in\mathbb F_p\) satisfy
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m u_jj^s=0\qquad(0\leq s<m), \tag{4}
\]
then all \(u_j\) are zero. This follows because the coefficient matrix \((j^s)_{0\leq s<m,\,1\leq j\leq m}\) is a Vandermonde matrix, whose determinant is
\[
 \prod_{1\leq r<s\leq m}(s-r),
\]
and none of its factors is zero modulo \(p\).

### A signed-binomial vector

For \(1\leq j\leq m\), define
\[
 b_j=(-1)^{m-j}\binom mj\in\mathbb F_p. \tag{5}
\]
The standard finite-difference identities say
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^m(-1)^{m-t}\binom mt t^s=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&0\leq s<m,\\
 m!,&s=m.
 \end{cases} \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, the left side is the \(m\)-th forward difference at \(0\) of the polynomial \(x^s\). Each forward difference lowers degree by one; it therefore vanishes after \(m\) differences if \(s<m\), while the \(m\)-th difference of \(x^m\) is the constant \(m!\). For \(s>0\), the omitted term \(t=0\) is zero, so (6) yields
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m b_jj^s=0\quad(1\leq s<m),
 \qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^m b_jj^m=C. \tag{7}
\]
For \(s=0\), the complete binomial sum is \((1-1)^m=0\); removing the \(t=0\) term gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m b_j=-(-1)^m=(-1)^{m+1}. \tag{8}
\]

We shall repeatedly use the following interpolation argument.

### Kernel-polynomial principle

Suppose a matrix over \(\mathbb F_p\) has entries
\[
 H_{ij}=(i^2-dj)^m\qquad(1\leq i,j\leq m), \tag{9}
\]
where \(d\ne0\), and suppose \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)^T\) lies in its kernel. Define
\[
 P(X)=\sum_{j=1}^m v_j(X-dj)^m. \tag{10}
\]
Then \(\deg P\leq m\), and the kernel relation says
\[
 P(i^2)=0\qquad(1\leq i\leq m).
\]
Let \(c\) be the coefficient of \(X^m\) in \(P\). Because \(X^m-1\) vanishes at the same \(m\) distinct nodes by (3),
\[
 D(X)=P(X)-c(X^m-1)
\]
has degree less than \(m\) and has the \(m\) distinct roots \(1^2,\ldots,m^2\). Therefore \(D=0\), and hence
\[
 P(X)=c(X^m-1). \tag{11}
\]
The same argument applies with \(X+dj\) in place of \(X-dj\).

We will also use that for \(0\leq k\leq m<p\), \(\binom mk\) is nonzero in \(\mathbb F_p\). Indeed, if \(p\mid\binom mk\), then the identity
\[
 \binom mk k!(m-k)!=m!
\]
would imply \(p\mid m!\), which is impossible because \(m<p\).

## 2. Nonvanishing when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)

Euler's criterion says that for every \(x\in\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \chi(x)=x^{(p-1)/2}=x^m. \tag{12}
\]
Thus reducing the integer matrix \(A\) modulo \(p\) gives the matrix
\[
 H_{ij}=(i^2-Cj)^m. \tag{13}
\]
We prove that \(H\) is invertible. This will imply that \(\det A\not=0\), since an integer determinant that were zero would certainly reduce to zero modulo \(p\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(H\) has a nonzero kernel vector \(v=(v_j)\). Set
\[
 P(X)=\sum_{j=1}^m v_j(X-Cj)^m.
\]
By the kernel-polynomial principle,
\[
 P(X)=c(X^m-1) \tag{14}
\]
for some \(c\in\mathbb F_p\).

Comparing coefficients gives precise information about the moments of \(v\). The leading coefficient gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m v_j=c. \tag{15}
\]
For \(1\leq s<m\), compare the coefficient of \(X^{m-s}\). On the right side of (14) this coefficient is zero. On the left it is
\[
 \binom m{m-s}(-C)^s\sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^s.
\]
The binomial coefficient and \(C\) are nonzero, so
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^s=0\qquad(1\leq s<m). \tag{16}
\]
Finally, comparison of constant terms gives
\[
 (-1)^mC^m\sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^m=-c. \tag{17}
\]

If \(c=0\), equations (15) and (16) say that all moments of orders \(0,1,\ldots,m-1\) vanish. The Vandermonde argument (4) then gives \(v=0\), contrary to our choice of \(v\).

It remains to rule out \(c\ne0\). Put
\[
 \sigma=(-1)^{m+1},\qquad \lambda=c\sigma.
\]
Since \(\sigma^2=1\), equations (8), (15), (16), and (7) show that the vectors \(v\) and \(\lambda b\) have the same moments of orders \(0,1,\ldots,m-1\): their zeroth moments are both
\[
 \lambda\sum b_j=\lambda\sigma=c,
\]
and all their moments of orders \(1,\ldots,m-1\) are zero. By the Vandermonde argument,
\[
 v_j=\lambda b_j\qquad(1\leq j\leq m). \tag{18}
\]
Here \(\lambda\ne0\), because \(c\ne0\). By (7),
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^m=\lambda C.
\]
Substituting this into (17) gives
\[
 (-1)^m C^{m+1}\lambda=-c.

after using \(c=\lambda\sigma=\lambda(-1)^{m+1}\), the right side equals \((-1)^m\lambda\). Cancelling the nonzero factor \((-1)^m\lambda\), we obtain
\[
 C^{m+1}=1. \tag{19}
\]

Now assume \(p\equiv1\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is even, so \(m+1\) is odd, and (2) gives \(C^2=-1\). Squaring (19), we get
\[
 1=(C^{m+1})^2=(C^2)^{m+1}=(-1)^{m+1}=-1,
\]
which is impossible in the field \(\mathbb F_p\), since \(p\ne2\). Thus \(H\) is invertible, and consequently
\[
 \det A\ne0\qquad\text{when }p\equiv1\pmod4. \tag{20}
\]

## 3. Quadratic-character sums

For the converse direction we need a standard character-sum calculation. We include its derivation.

For \(d\in\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(x^2-d)=
 \begin{cases}
 p-1,&d=0,\\
 -1,&d\ne0.
 \end{cases} \tag{21}
\]
If \(d=0\), the term at \(x=0\) is zero and every other term is \(1\), proving the first case.

For \(d\ne0\), one way to obtain the second case is to group the sum by \(y=x^2\). The number of square roots of \(y\) in \(\mathbb F_p\) is \(1+\chi(y)\). Therefore
\[
 \sum_x\chi(x^2-d)
 =\sum_y(1+\chi(y))\chi(y-d).

after expansion, the first sum \(\sum_y\chi(y-d)\) is zero, because translation permutes the field and a nontrivial multiplicative character sums to zero. The remaining sum is
\[
 \sum_y\chi(y(y-d)).
\]
Replacing \(y\) by \(du\), and using that \(\chi(d^2)=1\), reduces this to
\[
 \sum_u\chi(u(u-1))=-1. \tag{22}
\]
For completeness, (22) is the elementary quadratic Jacobi sum. It can also be counted directly: the number \(N\) of pairs \((r,u)\) satisfying \(r^2=u(u-1)\) is
\[
 N=\sum_u(1+\chi(u(u-1)))=p+\sum_u\chi(u(u-1)).
\]
Multiplying the equation by \(4\) and setting \(x=2u-1\), \(y=2r\), it becomes \(x^2-y^2=1\), or \((x-y)(x+y)=1\). Every nonzero value of \(x-y\) uniquely determines \(x+y\), and since \(2\) is invertible this uniquely determines \((x,y)\). Hence \(N=p-1\), proving (22) and thus (21).

It follows by completing the square that if \(a\ne0\), then
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(ax^2+bx+c)
 =
 \begin{cases}
 \chi(a)(p-1),&b^2-4ac=0,\\
 -\chi(a),&b^2-4ac\ne0.
 \end{cases} \tag{23}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 ax^2+bx+c
 =a\left(\left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2- rac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2}\right).
\]
Translation by \(b/(2a)\) permutes \(\mathbb F_p\), multiplicativity extracts the factor \(\chi(a)\), and (21) applies. This proves (23).

## 4. A partner matrix when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)

Assume from now on that
\[
 p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
Then \(m\) is odd. By (2), \(C^2=1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), hence \(C=1\) or \(C=-1\). Choose the ordinary integer
\[
 \varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}
\]
whose residue modulo \(p\) is \(C\). Thus
\[
 \varepsilon=C\text{ in }\mathbb F_p,
 \qquad \varepsilon^2=1,
 \qquad \varepsilon C=C^2=1. \tag{24}
\]
Define the integer partner matrix
\[
 B=(B_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq m},
 \qquad
 B_{ij}=\left(\frac{i^2+\varepsilon j}{p}\right). \tag{25}
\]
We first prove that \(B\) is nonsingular.

### Invertibility of the partner matrix

By Euler's criterion, the reduction of \(B\) modulo \(p\) is
\[
 K_{ij}=(i^2+\varepsilon j)^m. \tag{26}
\]
Suppose \(Kv=0\) for a vector \(v=(v_j)\in\mathbb F_p^m\), and define
\[
 R(X)=\sum_{j=1}^m v_j(X+\varepsilon j)^m.
\]
The kernel-polynomial principle again gives
\[
 R(X)=c(X^m-1) \tag{27}
\]
for some \(c\in\mathbb F_p\). Comparing coefficients exactly as before, now with \(+\varepsilon j\) instead of \(-Cj\), yields
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m v_j=c, \tag{28}
\]
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^s=0\qquad(1\leq s<m), \tag{29}
\]
and, from the constant coefficient,
\[
 \varepsilon^m\sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^m=-c. \tag{30}
\]
Here the factors \(\binom m{m-s}\) and \(\varepsilon^s\) that are cancelled in deriving (29) are nonzero.

Because \(m\) is odd, (8) gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m b_j=(-1)^{m+1}=1.
\]
Equations (7), (28), and (29), followed by the Vandermonde argument, therefore show
\[
 v_j=cb_j\qquad(1\leq j\leq m). \tag{31}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^m=cC.
\]
Also, since \(m\) is odd and \(\varepsilon^2=1\), we have \(\varepsilon^m=\varepsilon\). Substituting into (30) and using (24), we find
\[
 -c=\varepsilon(cC)=c.
\]
Thus \(2c=0\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(2\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), so \(c=0\), and then (31) gives \(v=0\). Hence \(K\) is invertible. It follows that the integer determinant \(\det B\) is nonzero: in fact, its reduction modulo \(p\) is the nonzero determinant of \(K\). Thus
\[
 \det B\ne0. \tag{32}
\]

### The product \(AB^T\) is skew-symmetric

Since \(C\equiv\varepsilon\pmod p\), the entries of \(A\) can be written as
\[
 A_{ij}=\chi(i^2-\varepsilon j),
 \qquad
 B_{ij}=\chi(i^2+\varepsilon j). \tag{33}
\]
Let
\[
 S=AB^T.
\]
For \(1\leq i,k\leq m\), multiplicativity of \(\chi\) gives
\[
 S_{ik}=\sum_{j=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((i^2-\varepsilon j)(k^2+\varepsilon j)\bigr). \tag{34}
\]
We will show that \(S_{ik}+S_{ki}=0\).

The nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_p\) are exactly
\[
 \{1,2,\ldots,m\}\ \dot\cup\ \{-1,-2,\ldots,-m\}. \tag{35}
\]
Indeed, each set has \(m\) distinct elements; they are disjoint because an equality \(i=-j\) would imply \(i+j=p\), contrary to \(i+j\leq p-1\); together they therefore contain all \(p-1=2m\) nonzero elements.

In the expression for \(S_{ki}\), replace a positive index \(j\) by the field element \(-j\) and commute the two factors. Combining (34) for \(S_{ik}\) and \(S_{ki}\), and using the partition (35), gives
\[
 S_{ik}+S_{ki}
 =\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p^*}
 \chi\bigl((i^2-\varepsilon t)(k^2+\varepsilon t)\bigr). \tag{36}
\]
Equivalently, on inserting the missing term \(t=0\),
\[
 S_{ik}+S_{ki}
 =\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}
 \chi\bigl((i^2-\varepsilon t)(k^2+\varepsilon t)\bigr)
 -\chi(i^2k^2). \tag{37}
\]
The last character value is \(1\), since \(i\) and \(k\) are nonzero:
\[
 \chi(i^2k^2)=1. \tag{38}
\]

It remains to compute the complete sum in (37). Put
\[
 a=i^2,
 \qquad b=k^2.
\]
Both are nonzero. Using \(\varepsilon^2=1\), we expand
\[
 (a-\varepsilon t)(b+\varepsilon t)
 =-t^2+\varepsilon(a-b)t+ab. \tag{39}
\]
As a quadratic polynomial in \(t\), its leading coefficient is \(-1\), and its discriminant is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Delta
 &=\varepsilon^2(a-b)^2-4(-1)ab\\
 &=(a-b)^2+4ab\\
 &=(a+b)^2. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{40}
\]
This discriminant is nonzero. For if \(a+b=0\), then
\[
 i^2=-k^2,

after division by the nonzero square \(k^2\), this would say that \(-1\) is a square modulo \(p\). But Euler's criterion gives
\[
 \chi(-1)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}=(-1)^m=-1
\]
because \(m\) is odd. Thus \(-1\) is not a square, a contradiction.

We may therefore apply the nonzero-discriminant case of (23) to (39). It gives
\[
 \sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}
 \chi\bigl((a-\varepsilon t)(b+\varepsilon t)\bigr)
 =-\chi(-1)=1. \tag{41}
\]
Combining (37), (38), and (41), we conclude that
\[
 S_{ik}+S_{ki}=1-1=0.
\]
Thus
\[
 S^T=-S; \tag{42}
\]
that is, \(S=AB^T\) is skew-symmetric.

### Odd skew-symmetric determinant

The order of \(S\) is \(m\), which is odd. For any skew-symmetric \(m\times m\) matrix over the integers,
\[
 \det S=\det S^T=\det(-S)=(-1)^m\det S=-\det S.
\]
Hence \(2\det S=0\), and over the integers this implies
\[
 \det S=0. \tag{43}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 \det S=\det(AB^T)=\det A\,\det(B^T)=\det A\,\det B.
\]
By (32), \(\det B\ne0\). Since the integers have no zero divisors, (43) forces
\[
 \det A=0\qquad\text{when }p\equiv3\pmod4. \tag{44}
\]

## 5. Conclusion

Every odd integer is congruent to either \(1\) or \(3\) modulo \(4\). Since \(p=p_n\) is an odd prime for every \(n\geq2\), these are the only two cases. In the first case, (20) gives \(\det A\ne0\); in the second, (44) gives \(\det A=0\). Therefore
\[
 a(n)=\det A=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p_n\equiv3\pmod4
\]
for every \(n\geq2\), as claimed.
